The visual/metric picture is now consistent: the `22°`, gain-`0.75`, guard-`28` anchor takes the most compact route and generates the strongest sampled upstream-relative x motion. Raising amplitude to `22.25°` still captures, but slows arrival and raises joint speeds and force/moment loads. I’m checking the inherited acceleration-guard probe next, since it isolates whether clipping authority or posterior transients are the better lever.

The inherited `28→29 rad/time²` guard probe also regressed: it took a visibly deeper correction, arrived at `80.00` instead of `74.23`, reduced upstream-relative x speed, and raised RMS force/moment to `33.84/488.89`. The candidate hypothesis is therefore an isolated posterior-transient test: preserve the proven anterior oscillator and its `28` guard, but lower only the posterior acceleration guard to `27` to reduce tail-driven yaw/load without reducing the anterior propulsion command. Per the visual-signals skill, I’m recording this diagnosis before touching the policy.

The single candidate is now in place with separate candidate-owned anterior/posterior guards (`28/27`), and the durable guidance now records both failed “more authority” probes plus their applicability boundary. I’m running the required workspace check next; this validates the policy contract and parameter schema without launching CFD.
